events.description: All systems connecting to DynamoDB in us-east-1 via the public endpoint began experiencing DNS failures; the regional DynamoDB DNS record was empty after the active plan was deleted. Global table replicas in other Regions saw prolonged replication lag.
EC2 DWFM state checks began to fail because the process depends on DynamoDB; droplet leases slowly timed out between 11:48 PM and 2:24 AM.
ECS, EKS and Fargate began experiencing container launch failures and cluster scaling delays (through 2:20 PM).
Redshift query and cluster operations began failing while DynamoDB endpoints were down (through 2:21 AM Oct 20; some clusters until 4:05 AM Oct 21).
AWS Support Center failed over to another region as designed, but an account metadata subsystem returned invalid responses blocking legitimate users (through 2:40 AM Oct 20).
Lambda began experiencing DynamoDB-related issues preventing function creation, updates, and causing invocation errors (through 2:15 PM Oct 20).
STS began returning API errors (recovered at 1:19 AM, then errors again 8:31-9:59 AM Oct 20).
AWS Management Console sign-in began failing for IAM users due to DynamoDB issues (through 1:25 AM Oct 20).
Amazon Connect began experiencing elevated errors handling calls, chats and cases (through 1:20 AM Oct 20; second period from 7:04 AM).
Engineers identified DynamoDB's DNS state as the source of the outage.
Temporary mitigations enabled some internal services to connect to DynamoDB and repaired key internal tooling, unblocking further recovery.
Recovery of ECS, EKS and Fargate container launches and cluster scaling completed (outage window ended at 2:20 PM).
All DNS information for DynamoDB was restored.
With DynamoDB recovered, DWFM began re-establishing leases across the EC2 fleet; EC2 APIs returned 'insufficient capacity' errors and new launches began failing (through 10:36 AM).
Customers could resolve the DynamoDB endpoint and connect as cached DNS records expired.
All global table replicas were fully caught up.
Engineers throttled incoming work and began selective restarts of DWFM hosts, clearing queues and allowing leases to be established.
Lambda's internal subsystem polling SQS queues, which had failed and not recovered automatically, was restored.

DWFM had established leases with all droplets in us-east-1; new launches started to succeed, though many saw 'request limit exceeded' errors due to throttling. Network Manager began propagating network configurations to newly launched instances, with a significant backlog.
Network Load Balancer began experiencing increased connection errors for some load balancers (through 2:09 PM).
Network Manager latencies increased as it worked through the backlog; new instances could launch but lacked network connectivity. Engineers worked to reduce load on Network Manager.
Monitoring detected NLB health check issues caused by alternating health check results for new EC2 instances brought into service before network state propagated; engineers began remediation.

From this time, NLB health check failures triggered Lambda instance terminations, leaving Lambda under-scaled; engineers throttled asynchronous work. Amazon Connect experienced a second period of errors due to NLB and Lambda impact.
Engineers disabled automatic health check failover for NLB, bringing healthy nodes and targets back into service and resolving connection errors.
Network propagation times returned to normal and new EC2 launches operated normally (some newly launched instances had connectivity issues until 1:50 PM).
Engineers began relaxing request throttles.
All EC2 APIs and new instance launches were operating normally.
Automatic DNS health check failover for NLB was re-enabled after EC2 recovery.
The event ended (overall end time, as stated in the overview).
